title: Standing against antisemitism
hookLine: naming hatred calmly and standing together
tomorrow: closing night, and someone mocks Tali's accent. Noa's fight?

cards: A "joke" lands in a group chat: an old line about Jews and money, with a laughing face. A couple of people react. Nobody types anything.
What do you say back? The tradition's first answer is: something. Leviticus puts it in one commandment, in the JPS 1917 translation: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour."

teach.b: Naming hatred calmly can be short: that's an old stereotype about Jews, and it isn't funny. No speech needed.

Then, if it helps, one fact, from the source. Some people hear chosen people as Jews thinking they're better. Deuteronomy says God didn't choose them for being many; they were the fewest of all peoples.
Hillel's questions in Pirkei Avot hold both halves of standing up: if I am not for myself, who will be for me?

teach.h: IF I AM ONLY FOR MYSELF…
teach.b: And if I am only for myself, what am I? Standing together runs both ways. Now a question under all of it: how much is one person worth?

The Mishnah answers that whoever destroys a single life is as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one, as if they saved a whole world. A neighbor tradition says it too, in its own book.
The Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, calls it a decree for the Children of Israel: "whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind."
Shared: one person weighs as much as humanity. Honestly different: the Mishnah draws it from Adam, created alone; the Qur'an sets it after the story of Adam's two sons, and names its own exceptions.
Jews and Muslims each read it in their own scripture.

how: Many synagogues, schools and Jewish groups teach calm ways to answer antisemitic myths, and build friendships with churches, mosques and neighbors who stand with them, as they stand with others.

o: a yearly day of fasting for past persecutions
avoiding anyone who disagrees with Jewish practice
calmly naming hatred of Jews and standing together

p: if I am only for myself, what am I?

s: in the Torah, God chose Israel for being many and mighty
Deuteronomy says they were the fewest of all peoples.
the Qur'an teaches that saving one life is like saving all mankind
Surah 5:32 calls it a decree for the Children of Israel, close to the Mishnah's 'a whole world.'
standing against antisemitism means long arguments with everyone
it can be one calm sentence, one true fact, and standing together.

games.q: a classmate says, half joking, that 'chosen people' means Jews think they're better. what's the calmest true answer?
o: Deuteronomy says they weren't chosen for being many; they were the fewest of all peoples.
everybody thinks they're better than everyone else, so it doesn't really matter.
ignore it: facts never change anyone's mind about this kind of thing.
games.why: one calm fact from the source answers the myth: Deuteronomy 7:7 says the choice wasn't about being greater or more numerous.

practice: Say one calm sentence out loud, the kind you could use when a joke targets anyone: that's a stereotype, and it isn't funny. Say it again, slower, at an ordinary volume, until it sounds like your own voice.
Calm is a skill, and it gets easier with practice.

wordCard.voice: Standing against antisemitism: naming hatred of Jews calmly, answering a myth with a fact, and refusing to stand idly by alone.

orig.note: Hebrew: do not stand (idly by), from Leviticus 19:16.

carryVoice: The line for today: stand together, for yourself and for whoever is next to you. Thirteen days.
